title: What GDP Counts
short: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
trouble: Students count intermediate goods, used goods, stock purchases and transfer payments, which either counts things twice or counts things that were not newly produced.

blocks.html: The The Circular Flow showed that the economy's spending and income go around a loop. To measure how much an economy produces, economists count the spending on its output in a careful way. The result is gross domestic product, or GDP.
GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, usually a quarter or a year.

Each word in the definition keeps GDP from counting something twice or counting something that was not made. Market value means we add things up by their prices, so cars and haircuts can be combined in dollars. Final goods are sold to their last user; the flour inside a loaf of bread is already in the bread's price, so counting the flour too would double-count it. Produced in the period leaves out used goods, which were counted the year they were made. Within a country means location, not ownership: a Japanese-owned car plant in Kentucky adds to U.S. GDP.

items: Counted: new goods and services sold to households, businesses, government and foreigners; new homes; goods produced this year but still unsold (they count as additions to inventories).

Not counted: intermediate goods (already inside the final price), used goods, purchases of stocks and bonds (a change of ownership, not production), transfer payments such as Social Security checks (nothing is produced in return), and unpaid work at home.

blocks.name: ec-sort

cards.text: A new car built in Ohio this year
cards.why: A final good produced in the U.S. this year.

cards.text: Flour a bakery buys to bake bread
cards.why: An intermediate good: its value is already in the bread.
It was counted in the year it was made.

cards.text: A dealer’s commission on a used car
cards.why: The dealer’s selling service is new production.
A financial transaction: ownership changes hands, nothing is made.
A transfer payment: no good or service is bought.

cards.text: Laptops made this year, still in a warehouse
cards.why: Counted as an addition to inventories.

cards.text: Cars made in Kentucky at a Japanese-owned plant
cards.why: GDP counts production inside the country, whoever owns the plant.

blocks.cap: Sort each item, then press Check. Each answer comes with a reason.

blocks.title: Which purchases add to GDP?
blocks.q: This year a family buys a newly built house for \$300,000, buys \$5,000 of stock, and pays a real estate agent \$9,000 to help sell their old house. How much do these add to GDP?
steps: The new house is newly produced: \$300,000 counts (as residential investment).
The stock is a financial asset changing hands: it does not count.
The old house was counted when it was built, but the agent's service happened this year: the \$9,000 commission counts.

blocks.html: Counting intermediate goods, used goods, stock purchases or transfer payments. These either count the same production twice or count things that were not produced this period. Quick check: ask "was something newly made, in this country, this period, and sold to its final user?" If not, leave it out (but do count any new service attached to it, like a commission).
